Similar risks are faced by occupants experiencing extreme cold, resulting in an estimated 38,000 deaths yearly (“Low Indoor Temperatures and Insulation” 2018). Though causal research is ongoing, many studies indicate that children and elderly populations over 65 years of age are especially vulnerable to poor indoor thermal comfort conditions (Hughes et al. 7 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2019). It is vital to identify resilient solutions that address occupant needs for indoor thermal comfort. Currently, personal comfort devices such as space heaters or tabletop fans are commonly used. In some cases, advanced equipment controls (e.g., enhanced humidity control, IoT-based comfort control) are implemented, or mechanical heating and cooling systems are oversized, to address the need (Mallay 2024; O’Neill et al. 2024). These existing solutions can be difficult to implement due to cost, installation logistics, effectiveness, or practicality. A tiered approach is recommended and should first prioritize basic building design (e.g., site location, form, shape, orientation, and window sizes), followed by passive strategies appropriate for the local climate (e.g., use of thermal mass, dedicated solar rooms, and natural ventilation), and lastly mechanical heating and cooling systems. Care must be taken not to increase the operational cost of buildings as a result of the proposed technology, as major challenges to adoption typically include upfront costs and long payback periods. It is essential that solutions are affordable and address occupant needs. 2.2.2.3 Challenge This challenge asks student teams to improve occupant indoor thermal comfort in U.S. buildings (residential, commercial, new, or existing) in extreme climates or locations prone to extreme weather events by focusing on the environmental factors that determine individual satisfaction within indoor atmospheres. Teams should first build out a focused problem statement for a specific stakeholder group (i.e., by climate zone) and then develop a technical solution that meets the needs of building occupants. For example, students may consider solutions that can measure real-time thermal comfort in subarctic climates and adjust environmental controls accordingly. Solutions should also prioritize electrical grid and building reliability. Teams must develop technical and holistic solutions to address the problem and should include at least one nontechnical component (e.g., an economic, policy, or commercialization component). Solutions that only consider stand-alone nontechnical components will not be considered. Suggestions for the student teams include (but are not limited to) the following: • Real-time sensing and response to occupant indoor thermal comfort needs • Advanced humidity control and measurement of occupant comfort in high-humidity climates • Passive approaches, such as solar spaces and radiant slabs, that extend the period of thermal comfort following an extreme weather event • Fuel switching to optimize low-cost operation, low energy use, or air quality concerns • Load shifting methods to increase system efficiencies or shift electrical loads to off-peak times. 2.3 Energy Management Energy management is the process of strategically monitoring, controlling, and optimizing the use of energy resources
